Figure caption: Design and synthesis of ionizable lipids by Passerini reaction. (A) Schematic representation of the mechanism of P-3CR-based synthesis of ionizable lipids. (B) Elaborate structures of three constituents employed in a batch test for the synthesis of ionizable lipids in the P-3CR library, including carboxylic acid (headgroup), isocyanide (tail A), and aldehyde (tail B). (C) Schematic of the HTS of ionizable lipids based on P-3CR. (D) Classical formulations for the preparation of mRNA-LNPs.

Figure caption: Batch screening of lipids for Fluc mRNA (mLuc) delivery. (A) Schematic of in vivo orthogonal batch test of LNPs from P-3CR library by I.M. injection. (B) The head groups were classified according to their chemical structure and the corresponding LNPs were characterized for their physicochemical properties. (C and D) Batch 1 analysis identified the best-performing head groups (0.32 mg kg−1 mLuc, 16 LNP mixtures per mouse, n = 2). (E) Batch 2 study identified one top-performing lipid tail (A4) (0.08 mg kg−1 mLuc, 4 LNP mixtures per mouse, n = 2). (F) Batch 3 determined the individual lipids with optimal transfection potency (0.05 mg kg−1 mLuc per mouse, n = 2). (G and H) Histogram analysis of batches 1 and 2. (I) The lipid structures were identified by batch test and lipids after the chemical modification (lipid H2A4B3, H2A4B4, H2A4-Ole, and H2A4-Butly). (J and K) The final comparison with the benchmark MC3 and SM-102 (0.05 mg kg−1 mLuc per mouse, n = 3). Statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed Student’s t test. *P-value < 0.05, **P-value < 0.01, ***P-value < 0.005. Data are presented as mean ± SEM.

Figure caption: Ionizable lipid-mediated mRNA delivery mechanism correlation with lipid tail structure in model membrane endosomal escape studies. (A) Ionizable lipid H2A4B4 tends to adopt a molecular “cone” shape, promoting the formation of inverted phases like the hexagonal HII phase shown. (B) FRET assay to assess lipid membrane fusion (incubated with endosomal mimic at pH 5.5 in 37 °C for 60 min). (C) Representative fluorescent images after the lipid dissociation (DNB-PE: λex = 488 nm, λem = 520 nm). (D) Histogram analysis of lipid fusion efficacy in different time intervals (10, 30, and 60 min, n = 5). (E) Hemolysis analysis of variable lipid and LNPs in acidic and neutral pH conditions (n = 3). (F) Histogram analysis of hemolysis percentage in different pH conditions compared to the control group (n = 3). (G) Lipid structure with the top performing tail combination containing different spacers (number of methylene units = 2, 3, and 4). (H) LNPs formulated with mLuc were injected intramuscularly into mice (0.05 mg kg−1 mLuc per mouse, n = 3). (I) The quantification data reveal that among the three LNPs, A4B4-S3 LNP stands out as the most efficient delivery vehicle. Data are shown as mean ± SEM (n = 3). (J–L) The TNS fluorescence was normalized to assess the apparent pKa of various LNPs. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed Student’s t test. *P-value < 0.05, **P-value < 0.01, ***P-value < 0.005. Data are presented as mean ± SEM.

Figure caption: Ionizable lipid-mediated mRNA delivery mechanism correlations with lipid headgroup. (A) Diagram depicting the interactions between ribose phosphate complexes and ionizable lipids (A4B4-S3 and A4B4-S4). (B) The electrostatic potential distributions of the ribose-phosphate complexes, lipids A4B4-S3 and A4B4-S4 are shown. Regions with negative electrostatic potential are indicated in red, while regions with positive electrostatic potential are shown in blue. (C) The schematic diagram illustrates the docking interactions between lipid molecules and ribose-phosphate complexes. The green dashed lines indicate the presence of hydrogen bonds.

Figure caption: In vivo delivery of mCre and hEPO mRNA to mice through retro-orbital administration. (A) Schematic illustration of Cre-mediated mRNA delivery in the Ai9 reporter mouse. Ai9 mice were retro-orbitally administered with mCre LNPs (0.5 mg kg−1 mCre per mouse, n = 3). The livers were collected and analyzed by flow cytometry. (B) Representative fluorescence images of liver sections (Channel: tdTomato and DAPI, Scale bar: 250 μm). (C) Histogram analysis for fluorescence images, quantified by ImageJ. (D) Quantification of tdTomato+ hepatocytes, endothelial, macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells, and T cells (n = 3). (E) Schematic illustration of retro-orbital injection of hEPO-containing LNPs. After 6 h dosing, blood was collected. Plasma was isolated for further ELISA. (F) Histogram analysis for hEPO concentration by ELISA (0.25 mg kg−1 hEPO mRNA per mouse, n = 8). (G) The administration of A4B4-S3 hEPO LNPs was repeated every 7 d for a total of five doses, and plasma hEPO levels were measured by ELISA at different time points (0.25 mg kg−1 hEPO mRNA per mouse, blood was collected at 0, 6, 12, 24, and 48 h). Statistical significance was assessed using a two-tailed Student’s t test. *P-value < 0.05, **P-value < 0.01, ***P-value < 0.005. Data are presented as mean ± SEM.
